newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea plans to set up fund to handle bad loans.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea plans to set up fund to handle bad loans.

text.p: South Korea plans to set up a fund worth about 1.5 trillion won to help resolve the problem of bad loans in the economy, the finance ministry said on Wednesday.
The fund, to be financed mainly with contributions from banks, bond issues and borrowings, will be operated for five years, a ministry statement said.
It said the government was considering special legislation to set up the fund and an organisation to run it.
The organisation, with an initial paid-in capital of 100 billion won, would be formed by expanding and reshaping the state-run Korea Asset Management Corp, it added.
The fund would help "speed up and rationalise" the handling of bad loans, reduce losses of companies, banks and creditors and minimise disorder in the banking system, it said.
The organisation would buy bad debts from financial institutions and liquidate them after making them marketable and adding value, the statement said.
It would function as a "clinic" for companies facing financial trouble by supporting their rescue efforts and advising them on management.
The statement said the move would shore up financial institutions by strengthening their competitiveness. It would also smooth industrial restructuring by efficiently handling shaky companies.
The ministry estimated bad debts held by the nation's commercial banks at about 2.4 trillion won at the end of 1996, the statement said.
It described bad debt as meaning debt on which payment is doubtful.

It excludes debt overdue for more than six months but where payment is thought possible because collateral has been secured. Such "fixed" debt is estimated at 9.4 trillion won and would be packaged by the organisation for resale in the near future, the statement said.
At the end of 1996, bad debt and fixed debts made up 4.1 percent of outstanding bank credit, the statement said.
Under the proposed rescue plan, if a creditor bank determined a company was in trouble, it would be advised to sell property or other assets to the organisation.
The organisation, in turn, would pay off the bank on behalf of the company, the statement said.
The ministry would form a task force to work out details of the measure before sending it to parliament in the form of a bill this year.
